This page goes with **Chapter 23, Enharmonic Modulation** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/EnharmonicModulation.html). Read the chapter
there first; the examples on this page are the site's own and all of them play. Each section folds from its ▾.

An **enharmonic modulation** is a modulation whose pivot chord is a **pun**. The chord is written one way, but it sounds exactly like
a chord that would be spelled differently in another key, and the music goes on as if it had been spelled that way. The spelling on the
page is right in only one of the two keys; you have to imagine the other. Like *son* and *sun*, the sound is the same and the meaning
changes. (The chapter's own example is the line "this sun of York", heard as "this son of York".) The ordinary pivot chords of
[Chapter 22](modulation.qmd) are spelled the same in both keys; this is the case where they are not.

Two sounds do almost all the work: the dominant seventh with the [German sixth](augmented-sixths.qmd), and the fully diminished
seventh. There is a third, rarer one at the end.

## A dominant seventh is a German sixth {#v7-ger}

Take the dominant seventh chord A♭ C E♭ G♭ (V⁷ of D♭ major). Spell its top note F♯ instead of G♭ and you have A♭ C E♭ F♯: a **German
augmented sixth chord** (Ger⁺⁶₅) in C. Nothing sounds different; only the top note changes its letter. A V⁷ wants its root to fall a fifth
(A♭ to D♭); the German sixth wants its bass to fall a half step to the dominant (A♭ to G). So the same chord can lead to two keys,
**a half step apart**: here D♭ major and C (minor or major).

That gives a modulation either way. Written as a German sixth in C minor and then heard as V⁷, it goes up a half step to D♭ major.
Written as a V⁷ in D♭ and heard as a German sixth, it goes down a half step to C. Pick a key, a direction, and listen. In each example
the chord comes twice in a row: once as spelled in the first key, once respelled, then the new key's tonic.

<div class="em-ger"></div>

The book says the **top note** is the one usually respelled; less commonly the bottom three notes are respelled and the top note kept as
a common tone. The players here respell the top note.

Secondary dominants are reinterpreted this way too (V⁷/x as a German sixth, and the other way round). Because V⁷ on R belongs to the
key a fourth above R and a German sixth with ♭6 on R to the key a major third above R, the German's key is always the lower one. The
chapter's examples with a dominant seventh and a German sixth as the pivot are Tchaikovsky, *The Nutcracker*, "Waltz of the Flowers";
Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, II; and "On My Own" from *Les Misérables*.

## The fully diminished seventh has four keys {#dim7}

A fully diminished seventh is made of three minor thirds stacked, so it is symmetrical: there are only **three different** fully
diminished sevenths in all, and each one can be spelled four ways, each way with a different note as the leading tone. Each spelling
is vii°7 of a different minor key, and the four keys are a minor third apart. B D F A♭ is vii°7 of C minor; the same sound as D F A♭ C♭
is vii°7 of E♭ minor; E♯ G♯ B D of F♯ minor; G♯ B D F of A minor. The ear can't tell which one the composer has in mind until the
chord resolves, so a diminished seventh is the most flexible pivot there is.

**Resolving up.** Each spelling's leading tone rises a half step to its key's tonic and the chord settles on the minor tonic triad:

<div class="em-dim" data-set="0"></div>

**Resolving down.** The book also resolves the chord the other way: take one note and let it **fall a half step**; that note becomes the
**root of a dominant seventh** and the chord's other three notes are that dominant seventh's third, fifth and seventh. Four notes, four
dominant sevenths, four tonics (E♭, G♭, A and C for this chord). The buttons in the second row of the player above show each of them.

The other two diminished sevenths are this chord moved up a half step and up a whole step; the same two rows of buttons:

<div class="em-dim" data-set="1"></div>

<div class="em-dim" data-set="2"></div>

*Double sharps.* In the third set one of the minor keys is G♯ minor, whose leading tone is F𝄪 (a double sharp), written out rather than
avoided. A composer would more likely hear it as the A♭ minor spelling or a dominant seventh.

## The enharmonic German sixth {#en-ger}

The German sixth has a third way of being spelled. Its ♭3 (E♭ in C) can be written as ♯2 (D♯). The chord then reads A♭ C D♯ F♯: the
interval from the bass to the D♯ is a **doubly augmented fourth**, and some books call it the "chord of the doubly augmented fourth".
The spelling matters because of where the note goes: the D♯ rises a half step to the third of the next chord, E, so the chord goes to
a **major I⁶₄**; the plain German resolves to V or to the cadential I⁶₄. In the player the first bar is the German as usual, the second
is the same sound respelled, the third the I⁶₄.

<div class="em-engerman"></div>

## Which key does it lead to? {#quiz}

A chord is shown; work out the respelling and pick the key. For a diminished seventh, tick all four minor keys it can be vii°7 of
(the one it is written in counts). For a German sixth or a dominant seventh, pick the key the respelled chord leads to.

<div class="em-quiz"></div>

## Where it happens in real scores {#real}

The chapter's examples with a diminished seventh as the pivot include Beethoven, Piano Sonata Op. 13 (*Pathétique*), I, where a
vii°⁴₂ in G minor is reheard in E minor; Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, II, from C major to A major; and Schubert, *Schwanengesang*,
"Der Atlas", where a diminished seventh in G minor is reheard in B minor and never settles in G.

One of them is in the Analysed Scores Library, and the notes can be read off its score. The library's key data for the
*Pathétique*'s first movement change from g to e in the development, in **bar 137** (the viewer's own numbering). In the first half of that bar the bass is E♭ with
F♯, A and C above: vii°⁴₂ in G minor (the chord is in third inversion, E♭ the seventh, in the bass). In the second half the bass is C
with F♯, A and **D♯** above: the same four pitch classes, with the E♭ now written D♯, vii°⁴₂ in E minor. The next bar's chord begins on
D♯, the leading tone of E, and goes on in E minor.
[Open bar 137](analysed-scores/view.html?id=beethoven-sonata-8-1&bar=137) in the library: it is lit and scrolled to, and ▶ plays the movement.
The other two aren't in the library (the Beethoven symphony is for orchestra; Der Atlas is there as a song, but its chord labels don't
mark the pivot). The analysis data has no label for an enharmonic pivot, so no other piece is claimed here without its notes
having been read.

The chapter doesn't include common-tone modulation (it is in [Chapter 22](modulation.qmd#commontone)).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## For teachers

- **Spelling rules.** Every chord on this page is spelled by letter steps and semitones from its key, so each note has its one right
  spelling (E♯ and G♭ appear where they should, and a few double sharps). The leading tone of a minor key is the tonic lowered by a letter
  and a half step. A V⁷ on R belongs to the key a perfect fourth above R; the German sixth with ♭6 on R to the key a major third above R;
  the two keys are a half step apart.
- **The voicings** are one bass note and three upper voices moving as little as possible (a doubling chosen by the same rule). They are
  not checked for every part-writing rule: the seventh of a V⁷ does not always fall, and parallel fifths may occur. The examples
  are for hearing the pun, not models of voice leading ([Chapter 29](voice-leading-chromatic.qmd) has the rules).
- **Tests.** `node tests/enharmonic/enharmonic.test.js` checks every spelling against semitone and letter arithmetic, and the drawn ABC
  (bar lengths, the sounding notes of each bar, the bass). `NEG=1` makes it fail.
- **Not here:** a chord-analysis level for chapter 23 (naming the pivot in both keys) needs two keys in one passage, which the
  chord-analysis engine, with one key per passage, doesn't have; and the book's Day One / Day Two exercises (notate and resolve a chord
  and its respellings) are only partly covered by the players and the quiz.
- The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
:::
